description: We're Starfire and all-girls team of engineering students taking on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge.
summary: Pluto was discovered when an astronomer flipped through two images of the same patch in the sky, noticing one dot that shifted. Starfire’s Flipbook allows anyone to employ this astronomers trick to NASA’s SPHERx telescope. The user just needs to enter a set of coordinates, or choose from the 5 suggested targets, select their desired field of view and one of the 6 SPHEREx detectors and the tool pulls real SPHEREx images directly from NASA’s IRSA archive, playing them like a flip-book, allowing users to see motion and spot changes in brightness to detect an object. Users can blink through every exposure, stack into a cleaner image, and subtract one epoch from another to narrow down to only the observed changes. Also generated is a brightness chart to help users track variable stars, with data-quality flags shown per frame as well as an optional proper-motion setting that centers the view on faster moving objects like Barnard’s Star. Every generated flip-book also creates a sharable link and an embed mode for anyone to use in their own sets. This tool is important, as it makes the exploration of our universe more publicly accessible, where just how astronomers first discovered Pluto, anyone can explore SPHERx’s large pool of data and make real observations.
details:
Features 

Starfire’s Flipbook public-facing web tool that creates a “flip-book” of images taken by NASA’s SPHEREx telescope for a specific location, allowing users to observe and detect objects. The user can enter RA and Dec coordinates or pick one of the five built in targets. They can then select the detector and field of view. The tool then queries NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive and downloads FITS image cutouts, parses them in the browser, then resamples every exposure onto a common north-up grid. Each frame also gets background subtraction and a stretch for display, resulting in a flip-book animation, with play, pause, step and speed and brightness controls. Users are encouraged to be real astronomers, allowing them to view every exposure, one stacked image per epoch, or each epoch minus the first or last. A brightness over time chart is also generated, useful for variable stars. A data-quality flag percentage, an optional proper-motion setting and link to Aladin Lite are also included. 

Benefits and intended impact
This tool requires no account of installation, allowing anyone to use it on any device, on any browser. Every generated flipbook also has a shareable link and embed mode for anyone to use in their own pages. The goal of Starfires Flipbook is to allow anyone to be an astronomer, making SPHEREx data more accessible to the public, especially those looking for movers and variables. 

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework), a small Cloudflare Worker that relays requests to IRSA because browsers can’t call it directly, GitHub Pages hosting, and a Python/Astropy workflow in Google Colab to pre-generate saved example frames. Data: SPHEREx images from IRSA; target coordinates and proper motions were checked in SIMBAD. 

Creativity
The tool and flip-book interface was inspired by Starfire, an alien from a distant planet who fights crime on earth in the popular Teen Titans. This tool is designed to look like her flip-book, a technology she uses to observe the night sky, and now anyone can use her “alien technology”. The tool also takes the blink comparator technique behind Pluto’s discovery and builds it into an easy to use web tool for SPHEREx. Everything happens directly in the user's browser, the tool downloads raw FITS cutouts, reads them and lines up every exposure on the same coordinates without a server doing the image work. The flipbook also goes beyond just flipping frames, but allows users to stack each visit into a cleaner image, and even subtract one epoch from another to refine, also included is the brightness chart and proper motion option. Also included are 5 saved samples, Barnard’s Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi, RW Aurigae and R Draconis, giving users a place to test the tool, and also works even if NASA’s archive is busy, which the tool is designed to retry access and fall back on these saved samples. Overall the tool is fun, easy to use, and designed to make the user feel like an astronomer. 

Factors considered
Saves examples were added to ensure the tool works on some five coordinates, even if the archive is slow and can not be accessed in time. Data quality was also considered, with exposures that are mostly empty being skipped by default. Lastly, since SPHEREx only has about a year of data, making slow motion more subtle, our alignment ignores small distortion terms so stars near an exposure edge may be a few pixels off and changes in general may be harder to track.
